Reason: regular narrow-complex tachycardia with short RP, retrograde (inverted) P waves in inferior leads, 1:1 AV conduction, manifest preexcitation seen in sinus beats after a pause, and evidence of fusion between AV nodal and accessory-pathway conduction during adenosine effect.

2. Atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT) — Less likely but plausible. Reason: very rapid, regular narrow-complex tachycardia and apparent AV-nodal decremental conduction before termination; however presence of manifest preexcitation and accessory-pathway behavior favors AVRT.

3. Focal atrial tachycardia (low atrial focus) with 1:1 conduction — Possible. Reason: can produce narrow complex tachycardia with abnormal P-wave axis; less favored because the ECG features (preexcitation, fusion with aden- osine) point to an accessory-pathway–dependent reentry.

4. Junctional tachycardia (automatic or microreentrant) — Uncommon but consider. Reason: narrow complex tachycardia with retrograde atrial activation can mimic this, but accessory-pathway findings make this less likely.

5. Ventricular tachycardia with 1:1 retrograde conduction (rare presentation) — Least likely. Reason: would usually produce wide QRS complexes; the narrow complexes and accessory-pathway signs argue against ventricular origin.

Recommended next steps (confirmatory/management priorities): arrange electrophysiology study ± catheter ablation for accessory pathway if clinically appropriate, obtain a 12-lead ECG in sinus rhythm to document baseline preexcitation, and basic workup (ECG telemetry/ambulatory monitor, electrolytes, TSH, and transthoracic echocardiogram) to assess structural heart disease prior to definitive therapy.
